notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Population geography studies the spatial distribution, density, growth, composition and movement of population.
  • It examines how population characteristics vary from one region to another.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Population Geography → Distribution + Density + Growth + Composition + Migration

2. Population
  • Population means the total number of people living in a specified geographical area at a particular time.
  • Population size changes through:
  • Births.
  • Deaths.
  • Immigration.
  • Emigration.
3. Census
  • A census is the systematic enumeration of the population.
  • It collects demographic, social and economic information about people and households.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census → Official Population Enumeration

4. Census of India
  • India normally follows a decennial census system.
  • Decennial means once every ten years.
  • Census data are fundamental for:
  • Planning.
  • Administration.
  • Representation.
  • Resource allocation.
  • Demographic analysis.
5. First Census Attempt in India
  • The first non-synchronous census exercise in India was conducted in 1872.
  • It took place during the period of Lord Mayo.
📌 Must-Memorise

1872 → First Non-Synchronous Census

6. First Regular Synchronous Census
  • The first complete synchronous census of India was conducted in 1881.
  • It was undertaken during the period of Lord Ripon.
📌 Must-Memorise

1881 → First Synchronous Census → Lord Ripon

7. Census Interval
  • Regular census enumeration in India has traditionally been conducted at ten-year intervals.
8. Census Act
  • Census operations in independent India are conducted under the Census Act, 1948.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Census Act → 1948

9. Census Authority
  • Census operations are organised by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India.
  • It functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census → Ministry of Home Affairs

10. Census 2011
  • Census 2011 was India's 15th census in the continuous census series beginning in 1872.
  • It was the 7th census after Independence.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

2011 → 15th Census Overall + 7th After Independence

11. Population of India — Census 2011

According to Census 2011:

  • India's population was approximately 1.21 billion.
  • The final total was about 121.09 crore.
12. India's Global Population Importance
  • India has historically contained a very large share of the world's population despite having a much smaller share of global land area.
  • This creates considerable population pressure on land and resources in many regions.
13. Population Distribution
  • Population distribution refers to the way people are spread across a geographical area.
  • India's population is very unevenly distributed.
14. Densely Populated Regions

High population concentrations occur in:

  • Ganga Plain.
  • Brahmaputra Valley.
  • Coastal plains.
  • Major river deltas.
  • Urban-industrial regions.
15. Sparsely Populated Regions

Low population densities occur in:

  • Himalayan mountains.
  • Thar Desert.
  • Dense forest regions.
  • High plateaus.
  • Some northeastern hill regions.
  • Island interiors.
16. Physical Factors Affecting Population Distribution

Important physical factors include:

  • Relief.
  • Climate.
  • Soil.
  • Water.
  • Natural resources.
17. Relief and Population

Plains generally support higher population because they favour:

  • Agriculture.
  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Settlements.
  • Industries.
18. Mountain Population

Mountain areas generally have lower density because of:

  • Steep slopes.
  • Harsh climate.
  • Limited cultivable land.
  • Difficult transport.
19. Climate and Population

Moderate climatic conditions generally favour dense settlement.

Extreme climates such as:

  • Very cold.
  • Very hot.
  • Very dry.

usually support lower population density.

20. Water and Population

Reliable water supply attracts settlement.

Major population centres are often associated with:

  • Rivers.
  • Groundwater.
  • Lakes.
  • Coastal regions.
21. Soil and Population
  • Fertile soils support intensive agriculture.
  • Alluvial plains therefore support large rural populations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fertile Alluvium → Dense Population

22. Mineral Resources and Population

Mining regions may attract:

  • Workers.
  • Industries.
  • Transport networks.
  • Urban settlements.
23. Human Factors Affecting Distribution

Important human factors include:

  • Agriculture.
  • Industry.
  • Transport.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Employment.
  • Historical settlement.
24. Industrialisation and Population

Industrial regions attract people because they offer:

  • Employment.
  • Services.
  • Markets.
  • Infrastructure.
25. Population Density
  • Population density is the number of persons living per unit area.
📌 Formula

Population Density

= Total Population ÷ Total Area

Usually expressed as persons per square kilometre.

26. India's Density — Census 2011

According to Census 2011:

  • India's population density was 382 persons per square kilometre.
📌 Must-Memorise

India Density 2011 → 382 persons/km²

27. Population Density vs Population Size
  • Population size means total number of people.
  • Population density means number of people per unit area.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Large Population ≠ Necessarily Highest Density

28. Most Populous State — Census 2011
  • Uttar Pradesh was India's most populous state in Census 2011.
  • Its population was approximately 20 crore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Most Populous State → Uttar Pradesh

29. Least Populous State — Census 2011
  • Sikkim was the least populous state in Census 2011.
📌 Must-Memorise

Least Populous State → Sikkim

30. High-Density State — Census 2011
  • Bihar had the highest population density among the states in Census 2011.
  • Its density was about 1,106 persons per sq km.
📌 Must-Memorise

Highest Density State → Bihar

31. Lowest-Density State — Census 2011
  • Arunachal Pradesh had the lowest population density among the states.
  • Its density was about 17 persons per sq km.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lowest Density State → Arunachal Pradesh

32. Delhi Density
  • Delhi had a much higher population density than any state.
  • Therefore, questions must distinguish between:
  • States.
  • States and Union Territories together.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Highest Density State → Bihar

Very High Density UT/NCT → Delhi

33. Ganga Plain Population

The Ganga Plain supports dense population because of:

  • Fertile alluvial soil.
  • Flat relief.
  • Abundant water.
  • Agriculture.
  • Transport.
  • Historic urban centres.
34. Brahmaputra Valley Population
  • Population is concentrated mainly along the valley floor.
  • Surrounding mountains and flood-prone areas limit settlement in some locations.
35. Rajasthan Population Distribution
  • Western Rajasthan is sparsely populated because of aridity.
  • Population density increases toward:
  • Eastern Rajasthan.
  • Irrigated areas.
  • Urban centres.
36. Himalayan Population Distribution
  • Population is concentrated in:
  • Valleys.
  • Lower slopes.
  • Towns.
  • High mountains remain sparsely populated.
37. Peninsular Population

Population is concentrated around:

  • River valleys.
  • Industrial regions.
  • Irrigated plains.
  • Coastal belts.
  • Major cities.
38. Coastal Population

Coastal plains support population through:

  • Agriculture.
  • Ports.
  • Fishing.
  • Industries.
  • Urban centres.
39. Population Growth
  • Population growth means change in population size over time.
  • It may be:
  • Positive.
  • Negative.
  • Zero.
40. Absolute Population Growth

Absolute growth:

Population at Later Date − Population at Earlier Date

41. Population Growth Rate
  • Growth rate expresses population change as a percentage of the earlier population.
42. Decadal Growth Rate
  • Decadal growth rate measures percentage population change over ten years.
  • It is widely used in Indian census analysis.
43. Natural Increase

Natural increase:

Births − Deaths

Migration is excluded.

📌 Must-Memorise

Natural Increase = Births − Deaths

44. Actual Population Change

Actual population change depends on:

  • Births.
  • Deaths.
  • Immigration.
  • Emigration.
45. Birth Rate
  • Crude Birth Rate is the number of live births in a year per 1,000 population.
46. Death Rate
  • Crude Death Rate is the number of deaths in a year per 1,000 population.
47. Fertility
  • Fertility refers to actual reproductive performance in a population.
  • It is different from biological ability to reproduce.
48. Total Fertility Rate
  • Total Fertility Rate represents the average number of children a woman would bear under prevailing age-specific fertility rates.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

TFR → Average Children per Woman

49. Replacement-Level Fertility
  • Replacement-level fertility is the fertility level at which one generation broadly replaces itself.
  • It is commonly taken as approximately 2.1 children per woman under low-mortality conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Replacement Fertility → About 2.1

50. Mortality
  • Mortality refers to occurrence of deaths in a population.
  • Declining mortality contributes to population growth when fertility remains high.
51. Infant Mortality Rate
  • Infant Mortality Rate measures deaths of infants below one year of age per 1,000 live births.
📌 Must-Memorise

IMR → Deaths Under Age 1 per 1,000 Live Births

52. Maternal Mortality Ratio
  • Maternal Mortality Ratio relates maternal deaths to live births.
  • It is generally expressed per 100,000 live births.
53. Life Expectancy
  • Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live under prevailing mortality conditions.
54. Population Growth Phases in India

Indian demographic history is often divided into broad phases:

  • 1901–1921 → Stagnant or slow growth.
  • 1921–1951 → Steady growth.
  • 1951–1981 → Rapid growth.
  • After 1981 → Growth continued, but the rate began declining.
55. 1901–1921 Period

Population growth remained low because of:

  • Epidemics.
  • Famines.
  • High death rates.
  • Poor healthcare.
56. Year of Great Divide
  • 1921 is known as the Year of Great Divide in India's demographic history.
  • After 1921, population began showing sustained growth.
📌 Must-Memorise

1921 → Year of Great Divide

57. Why 1921 is Important

Before 1921:

  • Population growth was irregular and weak.

After 1921:

  • Population generally increased continuously from census to census.
58. 1921–1951
  • Population began growing steadily.
  • Mortality gradually declined.
  • Healthcare and sanitation slowly improved.
59. 1951–1981
  • India experienced rapid population growth.
  • Death rates declined much faster than birth rates.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rapid Growth → Falling Death Rate + Persistently High Birth Rate

60. Post-1981 Trend
  • Population continued increasing.
  • However, the percentage growth rate gradually declined.
  • Fertility decline became increasingly important.
61. Population Explosion — Concept
  • Population explosion refers to very rapid population growth over a relatively short period.
  • It generally results when death rates fall while birth rates remain high.
62. Demographic Transition
  • Demographic Transition Theory explains the shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates with socioeconomic development.
63. Early Demographic Stage

Characteristics include:

  • High birth rate.
  • High death rate.
  • Low population growth.
64. Early Expanding Stage

Characteristics include:

  • High birth rate.
  • Rapidly falling death rate.
  • Rapid population growth.
65. Late Expanding Stage

Characteristics include:

  • Falling birth rate.
  • Low death rate.
  • Slowing population growth.
66. Low Stationary Stage

Characteristics include:

  • Low birth rate.
  • Low death rate.
  • Low population growth.
67. Age Composition
  • Age composition means distribution of population among different age groups.
  • It affects:
  • Labour supply.
  • Education demand.
  • Healthcare demand.
  • Dependency.
68. Broad Age Groups

Population is often grouped into:

  • Children.
  • Working-age population.
  • Elderly population.

For many Indian demographic discussions:

  • Below 15 years → Young dependent population.
  • 15–59 years → Working-age population.
  • 60 years and above → Elderly population.
69. Working-Age Population
  • A large working-age population can provide economic benefits if people are:
  • Healthy.
  • Educated.
  • Skilled.
  • Employed.
70. Dependency Ratio
  • Dependency ratio compares dependent-age population with working-age population.
📌 Basic Formula

Dependents ÷ Working-Age Population × 100

71. Child Dependency
  • Child dependency refers to the burden represented by younger dependent age groups.
72. Old-Age Dependency
  • Old-age dependency increases as the share of elderly population rises.
73. Population Ageing
  • Population ageing occurs when the proportion of elderly people increases.
  • It is associated with:
  • Lower fertility.
  • Longer life expectancy.
74. Demographic Dividend
  • Demographic dividend is the potential economic benefit arising when the working-age population becomes relatively large compared with dependents.
📌 Must-Memorise

Demographic Dividend → Large Working-Age Share

75. Conditions for Demographic Dividend

Benefits require:

  • Education.
  • Skill development.
  • Employment.
  • Healthcare.
  • Productive investment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Large Youth Population Alone ≠ Demographic Dividend

76. Demographic Burden
  • If employment and skills do not grow adequately, a large working-age population may create:
  • Unemployment.
  • Underemployment.
  • Social pressure.
77. Population Pyramid
  • A population pyramid graphically represents age and sex composition.
78. Expansive Population Pyramid

Characteristics:

  • Broad base.
  • Large child population.
  • High fertility.
  • Rapid population growth.
79. Stationary Population Pyramid

Characteristics:

  • More balanced age groups.
  • Low population growth.
80. Constrictive Population Pyramid

Characteristics:

  • Narrow base.
  • Low fertility.
  • Ageing population.
81. Sex Composition
  • Sex composition refers to the proportion of males and females in the population.
82. Sex Ratio in India

Indian Census sex ratio is expressed as:

Number of Females per 1,000 Males

📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Sex Ratio → Females per 1,000 Males

83. India Sex Ratio — Census 2011
  • Census 2011 recorded a sex ratio of 943 females per 1,000 males.
📌 Must-Memorise

India Sex Ratio 2011 → 943

84. Highest State Sex Ratio — Census 2011
  • Kerala had the highest sex ratio among states.
  • It recorded 1,084 females per 1,000 males.
📌 Must-Memorise

Highest State Sex Ratio → Kerala

85. Lowest State Sex Ratio — Census 2011
  • Haryana recorded the lowest sex ratio among states in Census 2011, at 879 females per 1,000 males.
86. Child Sex Ratio
  • Child sex ratio refers to the number of girls per 1,000 boys in the 0–6 age group.
📌 Must-Memorise

Child Sex Ratio → 0–6 Years

87. India Child Sex Ratio — Census 2011
  • India's child sex ratio in Census 2011 was 919 girls per 1,000 boys.
88. Factors Affecting Sex Ratio

Sex ratio can be influenced by:

  • Mortality differences.
  • Migration.
  • Gender discrimination.
  • Sex-selective practices.
  • Healthcare access.
89. Literacy
  • Literacy is an important indicator of social development.
  • Census literacy is measured among persons aged seven years and above.
90. Census Definition of Literate Person

A literate person is someone aged seven years or above who can:

  • Read.
  • Write.

with understanding in any language.

📌 Must-Memorise

Literacy → Age 7+ + Read and Write with Understanding

91. Formal Education and Literacy
  • Formal schooling is not compulsory for a person to be considered literate.
  • Ability to only read without writing is insufficient under the census definition.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Can Read Only → Not Counted as Literate

92. India Literacy — Census 2011

According to Census 2011:

  • Overall literacy rate was about 74.04%.
  • Male literacy was about 82.14%.
  • Female literacy was about 65.46%.
📌 Must-Memorise

India Literacy 2011 → 74.04%

93. Literacy Gender Gap
  • Literacy rates have historically been higher among males than females.
  • Reducing this gap is an important social-development objective.
94. Highest Literacy State — Census 2011
  • Kerala had the highest literacy rate among states, at about 94%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Highest Literacy → Kerala

95. Lowest Literacy State — Census 2011
  • Bihar had the lowest literacy rate among states, at approximately 61.8%.
96. Literacy and Development

Higher literacy generally supports:

  • Better health awareness.
  • Higher labour productivity.
  • Lower fertility.
  • Greater social participation.
97. Work Participation
  • Work participation rate measures the proportion of total population engaged in economically productive work according to census definitions.
98. Worker — Census Concept

Census workers are commonly divided into:

  • Main workers.
  • Marginal workers.
99. Main Worker
  • A main worker is a person who worked for six months or more during the reference year.
📌 Must-Memorise

Main Worker → 6 Months or More

100. Marginal Worker
  • A marginal worker worked for less than six months during the reference year.
📌 Must-Memorise

Marginal Worker → Less Than 6 Months

101. Census Occupational Categories

Workers are broadly classified as:

  • Cultivators.
  • Agricultural labourers.
  • Household-industry workers.
  • Other workers.
102. Cultivator
  • A cultivator operates land for agricultural production.
  • The person may own or lease the land.
103. Agricultural Labourer
  • An agricultural labourer works on another person's agricultural land for wages or payment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cultivator ≠ Agricultural Labourer

104. Household Industry Worker
  • Household industry workers engage in manufacturing, processing or related activity conducted mainly within the household setting.
105. Other Workers

This broad census category includes workers in activities such as:

  • Industry.
  • Trade.
  • Transport.
  • Government services.
  • Professional occupations.
106. Occupational Structure
  • Occupational structure refers to distribution of workers among different economic activities.
107. Primary Sector Population

Primary activities include:

  • Agriculture.
  • Forestry.
  • Fishing.
  • Mining.
108. Secondary Sector

Secondary activities include:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Construction.
109. Tertiary Sector

Tertiary activities include services such as:

  • Transport.
  • Trade.
  • Banking.
  • Education.
  • Healthcare.
110. Migration
  • Migration is movement of people from one place to another involving a change in usual residence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Migration → Change of Residence

111. Internal Migration

Internal migration occurs within a country.

It may be:

  • Rural to rural.
  • Rural to urban.
  • Urban to urban.
  • Urban to rural.
112. International Migration
  • International migration occurs across national boundaries.
113. Immigration
  • Immigration means movement into a country or region.
📌 Memory

Immigration → In

114. Emigration
  • Emigration means movement out of a country or region.
📌 Memory

Emigration → Exit

115. In-Migration
  • In-migration refers to movement into a region within the same country.
116. Out-Migration
  • Out-migration refers to people leaving a region for another region.
117. Net Migration

Net Migration:

In-Migrants − Out-Migrants

118. Push Factors

Push factors encourage people to leave their place of origin.

Examples include:

  • Unemployment.
  • Drought.
  • Poverty.
  • Conflict.
  • Natural disasters.
  • Low wages.
119. Pull Factors

Pull factors attract migrants to a destination.

Examples include:

  • Employment.
  • Education.
  • Higher wages.
  • Better services.
  • Urban opportunities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Push → Drives Out

Pull → Attracts In

120. Rural-to-Urban Migration
  • Rural-to-urban migration is strongly associated with:
  • Industrialisation.
  • Urban employment.
  • Education.
  • Services.
121. Rural-to-Rural Migration
  • Rural-to-rural migration includes:
  • Agricultural labour movement.
  • Marriage migration.
  • Seasonal movement.
122. Seasonal Migration
  • Seasonal migrants move temporarily for employment during particular periods.
  • Examples include:
  • Harvest labour.
  • Construction work.
  • Brick kilns.
123. Circular Migration
  • Circular migration involves repeated movement between origin and destination rather than permanent relocation.
124. Migration and Urban Growth

Migration can increase:

  • Urban population.
  • Housing demand.
  • Transport demand.
  • Employment pressure.
125. Benefits of Migration

Migration can:

  • Provide employment.
  • Increase household income.
  • Transfer skills.
  • Reduce labour shortages.
126. Remittance
  • Remittance is money sent by migrants to their families or communities of origin.
  • It can support:
  • Consumption.
  • Education.
  • Housing.
  • Investment.
127. Migration Challenges

Rapid migration can contribute to:

  • Housing shortages.
  • Congestion.
  • Informal settlements.
  • Pressure on water and sanitation.
128. Urbanisation
  • Urbanisation is the increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas.
  • It is associated with:
  • Industrialisation.
  • Services.
  • Migration.
  • Expansion of towns.
129. India Rural Population — Census 2011

According to Census 2011:

  • Approximately 68.84% of India's population lived in rural areas.
130. India Urban Population — Census 2011
  • Approximately 31.16% of India's population lived in urban areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

India Urban Population 2011 → 31.16%

131. Urban Population Growth

Urban population can increase through:

  • Natural population increase.
  • Migration.
  • Expansion of municipal boundaries.
  • Reclassification of rural settlements as urban.
132. Statutory Town
  • A statutory town is an urban settlement officially constituted under law.
  • Examples include areas governed by:
  • Municipal corporation.
  • Municipality.
  • Cantonment board.
  • Notified town authority.
133. Census Town

A Census Town is a settlement that is not legally notified as urban but meets census demographic and occupational criteria.

134. Census Town Criteria

The standard Census criteria include:

  • Minimum population of 5,000.
  • Population density of at least 400 persons per sq km.
  • At least 75% of male main workers engaged in non-agricultural pursuits.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census Town → 5,000 + 400/km² + 75% Male Main Workers Non-Agricultural

135. Urban Agglomeration
  • An urban agglomeration is a continuous urban spread consisting of:
  • A town with adjoining outgrowths.
  • Two or more contiguous towns.
  • Towns and their outgrowths.
136. Outgrowth
  • An outgrowth is an urbanised area physically adjoining a statutory town but lying outside its legal boundary.
  • Examples can include:
  • Railway colonies.
  • University campuses.
  • Port areas.
137. Metropolitan City
  • A metropolitan city generally refers to an urban area with a population of one million or more in Indian demographic discussions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Metropolitan → 10 Lakh+

138. Class I Town
  • Class I towns have a population of 100,000 or more.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Class I Town → 1 Lakh+

139. Class II Town
  • Population between 50,000 and 99,999.
140. Class III Town
  • Population between 20,000 and 49,999.
141. Class IV Town
  • Population between 10,000 and 19,999.
142. Class V Town
  • Population between 5,000 and 9,999.
143. Class VI Town
  • Population below 5,000.
144. Urban Sprawl
  • Urban sprawl is outward expansion of built-up areas into surrounding rural or peri-urban land.
145. Peri-Urban Zone
  • Peri-urban areas form a transition between urban and rural landscapes.
  • They experience rapid changes in:
  • Land use.
  • Population.
  • Employment.
146. Suburbanisation
  • Suburbanisation is population and development growth in areas surrounding the central city.
147. Conurbation
  • A conurbation forms when expanding neighbouring towns or cities physically merge into a continuous urban region.
148. Urban Heat Island
  • Built-up cities may be warmer than surrounding rural areas.
  • This is called the urban heat-island effect.
149. Urban Population Problems

Rapid urban growth can create:

  • Housing shortage.
  • Traffic congestion.
  • Air pollution.
  • Waste accumulation.
  • Water scarcity.
  • Flooding.
150. Informal Settlements
  • Informal settlements may develop where affordable formal housing is insufficient.
  • They often lack adequate:
  • Water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Drainage.
151. Urban Flooding and Population

High urban population density combined with:

  • Impervious surfaces.
  • Wetland loss.
  • Poor drainage.

can increase flood risk.

152. Population and Resources

Rapid population increase can place pressure on:

  • Land.
  • Water.
  • Forests.
  • Energy.
  • Housing.
  • Infrastructure.
153. Population Pressure

Population pressure becomes severe when population demand exceeds the capacity of available resources and infrastructure.

154. Carrying Capacity
  • Carrying capacity is the maximum population or activity level that an environment can support sustainably under specified conditions.
155. Population and Food

Population growth increases demand for:

  • Cereals.
  • Pulses.
  • Vegetables.
  • Fruits.
  • Milk.
  • Meat.
156. Population and Water

Growing population increases:

  • Drinking-water demand.
  • Irrigation demand.
  • Industrial water demand.
  • Wastewater generation.
157. Population and Land

Population growth can lead to:

  • Smaller farm holdings.
  • Urban expansion.
  • Conversion of agricultural land.
  • Greater housing demand.
158. Population and Environment

High resource consumption can contribute to:

  • Pollution.
  • Waste.
  • Deforestation.
  • Water stress.
  • Land degradation.

Population size is only one factor; consumption pattern and technology are also important.

159. Population Policy — Basic Concept

Population policies may seek to improve:

  • Reproductive health.
  • Maternal health.
  • Child health.
  • Education.
  • Family welfare.
160. Family Planning

Family planning enables individuals and couples to decide:

  • Number of children.
  • Spacing between births.
161. Population Stabilisation
  • Population stabilisation occurs when births and deaths become broadly balanced over the long term, accounting for migration.
162. Women's Education and Fertility

Higher female education is commonly associated with:

  • Later marriage.
  • Better health awareness.
  • Lower fertility.
  • Improved child health.
163. Infant Survival and Fertility
  • Improved child survival can contribute over time to smaller desired family size.
164. Population Quality

Population development depends not only on number of people but also on:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Skills.
  • Nutrition.
  • Employment.
165. Human Capital
  • Human capital refers to the productive abilities, knowledge and health of people.
  • Education and skill development increase human capital.
166. Population and Labour Force
  • Labour force includes persons who are employed or available and seeking work under the relevant statistical definition.
  • It is not identical to total working-age population.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Working-Age Population ≠ Labour Force

167. Workforce
  • Workforce refers to people actually engaged in economic activity under the relevant definition.
168. Labour Force Participation
  • Labour force participation measures the share of population participating in or seeking economic activity.
169. Population Momentum
  • Population momentum means population can continue growing even after fertility reaches replacement level.
  • This occurs when a large share of population is young and entering reproductive ages.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Population Momentum → Growth Due to Young Age Structure

170. Demographic Window
  • A demographic window occurs when the working-age share is relatively high and dependency is relatively low.
  • It can support faster economic growth if jobs and skills are available.
171. Population Ageing Challenge

Ageing increases demand for:

  • Healthcare.
  • Pensions.
  • Elder care.
  • Social security.
172. Rural Population
  • Rural populations generally have stronger dependence on:
  • Agriculture.
  • Natural resources.
  • Rural economic structures are becoming increasingly diversified.
173. Urban Population

Urban populations are concentrated in:

  • Industry.
  • Trade.
  • Transport.
  • Administration.
  • Service activities.
174. Population and Regional Inequality

Population characteristics vary greatly among Indian regions because of differences in:

  • Fertility.
  • Mortality.
  • Migration.
  • Economic development.
  • Urbanisation.

181. Tamil Nadu Population Distribution

Population is especially concentrated in:

  • Chennai metropolitan region.
  • Northern industrial corridor.
  • Coimbatore-Tiruppur-Erode belt.
  • Kaveri basin.
  • Madurai region.
182. Chennai Population Concentration

Chennai's dense population results from:

  • Port functions.
  • Industries.
  • Administration.
  • Services.
  • Education.
  • Transport connectivity.
183. Chennai Metropolitan Region
  • Chennai's urban influence extends beyond the core municipal area into surrounding suburban and peri-urban settlements.
  • This is an example of metropolitan expansion.
184. Coimbatore Population
  • Coimbatore is a major urban-industrial centre.
  • Engineering, textiles, education and services attract migrants.
185. Tiruppur Population Growth
  • Tiruppur's textile and garment industries attract migrant labour.
  • Industrial employment has contributed significantly to urban growth.
186. Hosur Population Growth
  • Hosur's proximity to Bengaluru and industrial development have encouraged rapid urbanisation and migration.
187. Madurai
  • Madurai is a major urban centre of southern Tamil Nadu.
  • Functions include:
  • Trade.
  • Education.
  • Healthcare.
  • Tourism.
188. Tiruchirappalli
  • Tiruchirappalli is an important central Tamil Nadu urban centre.
  • Its transport location supports population concentration.
189. Salem
  • Salem is an important industrial, commercial and transport centre of western-central Tamil Nadu.
190. Kaveri Delta Population
  • The Kaveri delta supports relatively dense rural settlement because of:
  • Fertile land.
  • Irrigation.
  • Paddy cultivation.
  • Historic settlement.
191. Nilgiris Population Pattern
  • Population density is lower than major Tamil Nadu plains because of:
  • Mountain relief.
  • Forests.
  • Protected areas.

  • Tamil Nadu has experienced substantial fertility decline and population ageing compared with many historically higher-fertility Indian regions.

provided adequate:

207. TNPSC Traps
  • Census and sample survey are not the same.
  • India's first census attempt was in 1872.
  • First regular synchronous census was in 1881.
  • 1921 is called the Year of Great Divide.
  • Population size and population density are different.
  • Uttar Pradesh has the largest population among states in Census 2011.
  • Bihar has the highest population density among states, not the largest total population.
  • Arunachal Pradesh has the lowest state density.
  • Sex ratio in India means females per 1,000 males.
  • Child sex ratio refers specifically to ages 0–6.
  • Literacy is calculated for persons aged seven years and above.
  • Merely being able to read is not sufficient for census literacy.
  • Main worker and marginal worker are different.
  • Main worker → Six months or more.
  • Agricultural labourer and cultivator are not the same.
  • Natural increase excludes migration.
  • Immigration means movement in.
  • Emigration means movement out.
  • Push and pull factors are different.
  • Urbanisation is a percentage/proportional concept, not simply an increase in city population.
  • Census Town and Statutory Town are not identical.
  • A large youth population does not automatically create a demographic dividend.
  • Working-age population and labour force are not the same.
  • Low fertility can eventually cause population ageing.
  • Population can continue growing after fertility falls because of population momentum.
  • Tamil Nadu was nearly half urban according to Census 2011.
